abstract: This paper examines how extremist political ideas travel from fringe movements into mainstream party politics via aligned intermediary networks that obscure their origins. Using a dynamic network analysis and time-series analysis of a German anti-immigration campaign ('Migrationspakt Stoppen') opposing the 2018 UN Global Compact for Migration, the authors trace how content originating with the small extremist Identitarian Movement spread through networks of low-level AfD party activists, 'superspreader' accounts, and far-right media sites before the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party leadership adopted it as an official campaign. The study shows that these intermediary networks 'launder' extremist content, allowing a radical-right party to take up and claim ownership of ideas it was officially pledged not to endorse, ultimately pushing extremist framing into mainstream media and public discourse.
key_claims: Radical-right parties can adopt ideas from extremist factions without formal coordination because aligned intermediary networks bridge movement and party actors who cannot openly endorse one another.
Intermediary networks act as 'source-laundering' mechanisms that disconnect content from its extremist origins and lend it political legitimacy.

The AfD's 'Migrationspakt Stoppen' campaign was a near-identical copy of the Identitarian Movement's campaign in framing, slogans, imagery (e.g., the ticking clock), and tropes (e.g., 'replacement migration'), despite no public reference to the movement.
Campaign networks grew non-linearly through staged 'handoffs' rather than steady concentric growth, with no single actor serving as the core mobilizer.
Such networked content flows make conventional standards for regulating harmful speech and demonstrating coordination difficult to apply, posing a novel threat to liberal democracy.
methods: Set up a multi-platform monitoring system of the German far-right media ecology tracking content from 11 July to 15 December 2018.
Dynamic network analysis (using Python, Gephi, and the ForceAtlas2 layout algorithm) of retweet networks, with nodes sized by indegree centrality and colored by actor type.
Time-series analysis of tweet and retweet volumes across actor categories using the campaign terms 'Migrationspakt' and 'Migrationspakt Stoppen' / 'stoppen'.

Collected data from YouTube (via R 'tuber' package: 1,606 videos from 681 channels), Twitter (via Crimson Hexagon: 506,079 tweets including 69,361 original tweets and 410,276 retweets from 43,579 accounts, ~60% of relevant traffic), far-right news/information sites (Media Cloud collections RNIS-DEU and RNIS-AUT, 21 sites), mainstream German media (Spiegel, Bild, FAZ, Tagesspiegel, Welt, Zeit), and the AfD party website and 'AfD Kompakt'.

Manual and semi-automated coding of accounts into actor types: mass media, far-right news sites, Identitarian actors, low-level AfD (224 accounts), high-level AfD (4 accounts), and top-100 superspreaders.
Bot detection on all accounts using Botometer with a 0.75 threshold (finding only 5.9% automated accounts producing 3.4% of tweets).
findings: Prior to the Identitarian campaign launch on 16 September 2018 there was only sporadic activity around the Global Compact for Migration.
After Identitarian leader Martin Sellner's launch video, the @migrationspakt account became the most-retweeted in the network within one day, and intermediary network activity spiked immediately.
Superspreaders constituted only 0.27% of network nodes but accounted for about 21% of all interactions, both amplifying and bridging separate networks.
Far-right news sites (RNIS) played a dual role: initial intermediaries bridging extremists and the party (visible more in original tweets than retweets), and later amplifiers of the party campaign.

The AfD launched a mirror-image official campaign in early October and a formal parliamentary petition on 1 November that gained over 100,000 signatures; the party then falsely claimed to be the sole originator of the GCM opposition.

Intermediary network activity escalated further after official AfD uptake; the overall network reached 23% of its final size during the October AfD launch and nearly doubled after the November petition.

Mainstream media covered the issue after the parliamentary petition but largely without the 'stoppen' campaign frame, focusing instead on the renewed CDU-CSU conflict over immigration; the most-retweeted post in the dataset came from Die Welt.
contributions: Introduces an empirical framework for tracing how extremist ideas move into mainstream politics through aligned intermediary networks, extending Klein's concept of 'information laundering' to movement-party dynamics.
Demonstrates a method combining multi-platform data collection with dynamic network and time-series analysis to detect network 'handoffs' without evidence of formal coordination.
Advances theoretical understanding of networked framing, networked agenda-setting, network monitoring, network alignment, and the role of superspreaders in hybrid media systems.
Provides a generalizable case relevant to other movement-party interactions (e.g., Trump/MAGA/QAnon in the US, Le Pen and the Gilets Jaunes in France, AfD and PEGIDA).
Highlights regulatory and democratic challenges posed by dispersed, networked spread of extremist content.
framing: The paper positions itself within political communication and social movement studies on the radical and extreme right, drawing on theories of hybrid media systems, networked framing and agenda-setting, movement-party interaction, and information laundering. It frames networked content flows as a distinctive contemporary threat to liberal democratic values, invoking debates about how democracies erode and about distinguishing dangerous communication from protected speech.
